#: Scrub manifest for the network collector: nft -j ruleset payloads (nft.json), the union across every variant — a populated ruleset, a metainfo-only empty one, and the canary plant. nftables JSON is one list of single-key objects (metainfo | table | chain | rule | set), so every entry starts nftables.*.
#nothing: Table and chain names are distribution conventions — filter, nixos-fw, ts-input — identical across every install of that distro or daemon, so they disclose nothing and substituting them would turn a specimen of a real firewall into a specimen of nothing (DESIGN 21). The same goes for hooks, policies, priorities, handles, counters, fwmark masks, protocol/field selectors and interface-name globs.
#comments: Rule and set comments are free text an operator can put anything into — content, and the canary variant plants a credential-shaped string in one precisely because this is a real leak surface.
#addresses: A match comparand (match.right) is usually a port, fwmark or protocol constant and occasionally a bare address; the classes live in one member, so it takes the free-text pass, whose address rules keep well-known constants and substitute everything else within its own space. {addr, len} prefixes are scrubbed as a unit so the base stays valid for its length — the /23 that came out base-invalid is the pinned regression.
#map: A named map is a top-level object like a table or a chain, and its `elem` list is a list of [key, verdict] PAIRS — which is why the two halves are classified apart. The verdict half is nftables' own vocabulary and takes the same `nothing` as the identical statement written inline in a rule. The KEY half is whatever the map is typed on: inet_proto here, an address or a port in the next capture, exactly the mixture match.right already holds — so it takes the same free-text pass rather than a `nothing` that would publish the first address somebody keys a map on. The map's own name stays for the reason a chain's does: it is the string the dispatching rule spells as @dispatch, and substituting one side of that join would leave a specimen of a map nothing consults.
#prefix.addr: Both families arrive at this one path (100.64.0.0 and fe80:: alike); the {addr, len} pair walk detects the shape itself and the substitution is family-aware, so the format here only says 'this is an address field' — which is also what arms the checker's in-space-replacements allowance.
#vmap.data: Two shapes at one path, and only one of them is a leaf: an INLINE map carries {"set": [...]} and walks the entries below, while a NAMED map is the bare string "@dispatch". The string is the other end of the map object's name — the whole of what makes the map-dispatched chain reachable — so it is classified with the name it refers to.
